implementation_notes: C's shotgun surgery is mostly about globals and macros: a new field means every `struct` that carries it, every `init` function that must zero it, and every consumer that reads it. The remedy is usually a struct with one definition and accessor functions, or a single table-driven approach; the discipline that keeps it from re-scattering is making the struct opaque and publishing only accessors. Because there is no compiler enforcement, the scattering returns silently as soon as one new consumer accesses the field directly.
idiom_name: one extern declaration per call site of a global
pitfalls: `extern` declarations of the same global across headers mean the compiler cannot tell you how many places assume its existence.
Initialising a new global in only one of three init paths is the classic silent miss that this refactoring is meant to make impossible.
Bit-fields in a shared struct make every addition a change to all users, which is shotgun surgery at the ABI level.
